title: N-Queens
tagline: Place queens row by row, pruning attacked squares — backtracking with constraint checks.

intuition.analogy: Seating n rival monarchs so none can attack another. You seat one per row, and before each placement you check that no earlier queen shares the column or a diagonal. If you get stuck, you un-seat the last queen and try the next square.
paragraphs: N-Queens places n non-attacking queens on an n×n board. Since each row holds exactly one queen, you decide a column for each row in turn — turning a huge search into a per-row choice.

The power is in pruning: a partial placement that already has a conflict can never become valid, so you cut that branch immediately. Constant-time conflict checks use sets for occupied columns and the two diagonal directions (row−col and row+col are constant along diagonals).
It's the archetypal constraint-satisfaction backtracker: assign, check feasibility, recurse, and undo on failure. The same skeleton solves Sudoku, graph colouring, and crosswords.
intuition.keyIdea: One queen per row; prune any column/diagonal conflict instantly, then backtrack on dead ends.

steps.title: Recurse by row
steps.detail: solve(row): if row == n, a full board is found. Otherwise try each column in this row.

steps.title: Check safety in O(1)
steps.detail: A column c is safe if c, row−c, and row+c are all unused. These capture column and both diagonals.

steps.title: Place, recurse, undo
steps.detail: Mark the three sets, recurse to the next row, then unmark (backtrack) to explore other columns.

complexity.timeReason: Worst case explores a factorial number of placements, but constraint pruning cuts most branches early.
complexity.spaceReason: Recursion depth n plus three sets of size ≤ n.

pitfalls: Diagonal encoding: cells on a '/' diagonal share row+col; on a '\\' diagonal share row−col.
Forgetting to remove markers on backtrack leaves phantom conflicts.
Generating boards (not just counting) needs to record the column choices per row.

dryRun.clickMoment: When row 2 has no safe column, the search abandons that whole subtree instantly and un-places the row-1 queen. That early pruning is why backtracking beats brute force enumeration.
